content.intro: Learn inserting data with insert through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Inserting Data With INSERT matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use inserting data with insert to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Basic INSERT INTO, Specifying column names, Inserting a single row, Inserting multiple rows. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Basic INSERT INTO
items.text: Basic INSERT INTO changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: Specifying column names
items.text: Specifying column names helps you insert, update, delete, synchronize, and return changed data safely, using bounded changes, staging, conflict handling, and transactions where needed. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Handling missing optional fields
items.text: Handling missing optional fields requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
